title: Fat, two carbons at a time

scenes.narration: Before a fat can fuel anything, it has to be unpacked in three deliberate stages. First, the triacylglycerols stored in adipose tissue are hydrolyzed by lipase, splitting each molecule into three free fatty acids plus a glycerol backbone, which travel out into the blood toward tissues that need energy. Second, those fatty acids are activated and shuttled across the mitochondrial membranes. Third, inside the matrix, the fatty acid is dismantled into acetyl-CoA units the citric acid cycle can burn. Keep this roadmap in mind. Release, activation and import, then degradation. Everything that follows is just detail filling in these three moves.
scenes.slideTitle: Three Stages of Fatty Acid Processing
scenes.notes: Before a fat can fuel anything, it has to be unpacked in three deliberate stages. First, the triacylglycerols stored in adipose tissue are hydrolyzed by lipase, splitting each molecule into three free fatty acids plus a glycerol backbone, which travel out into the blood toward tissues that need energy. Second, those fatty acids are activated and shuttled across the mitochondrial membranes. Third, inside the matrix the fatty acid is dismantled into acetyl CoA units the citric acid cycle can burn. Keep this roadmap in mind: release, activation and import, then degradation. Everything that follows is just detail filling in these three moves.

scenes.visual: carnitine passport across the inner membrane
scenes.narration: Activated fatty acids face a wall. Coenzyme A cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, so the acyl group needs a different passport to reach the matrix. That passport is carnitine. In step one, the fatty acid is activated to acyl CoA in the cytosol. Then carnitine palmitoyl transferase I swaps CoA for carnitine forming acyl-carnitine, which the translocase ferries across the inner membrane. On the matrix side, CPT II reverses the swap, handing the acyl group back to a fresh CoA so beta oxidation can begin. Carnitine itself is recycled back out. This shuttle is also the key regulatory checkpoint controlling fatty acid entry.

scenes.visual: number carbons; beta carbon is oxidized; chain cut
scenes.narration: The name beta-oxidation tells you exactly where the chemistry happens. Number the carbons starting from the carboxyl carbon as carbon 1. Carbon 2 is the alpha carbon, and carbon 3, the next one out, is the beta carbon. Beta-oxidation means we attack and oxidize that beta carbon, converting it to a keto group so the chain can be cleaved there. The delta notation is a companion convention. Delta N marks the first carbon of a double bond, so delta 2 means a double bond between carbons 2 and 3. Each round of oxidation generates acetyl-CoA, along with the reduced carriers NADH and FADH2, the energy currency we are after.
scenes.notes: The name beta oxidation tells you exactly where the chemistry happens. Number the carbons starting from the carboxyl carbon as carbon one. Carbon two is the alpha carbon, and carbon three, the next one out, is the beta carbon. Beta oxidation means we attack and oxidize that beta carbon, converting it to a keto group so the chain can be cleaved there. The delta notation is a companion convention: delta-n marks the first carbon of a double bond, so delta-two means a double bond between carbons two and three. Each round of oxidation generates acetyl CoA along with the reduced carriers NADH and FADH2, the energy currency we are after.

scenes.visual: ATP ledger for palmitate as a running bar
scenes.narration: Let's tally the payoff for fully oxidizing palmitate, a 16-carbon fat. Activation costs two ATP equivalents up front, so we start at minus 2. Seven rounds of beta-oxidation each yield 1 FADH2 and 1 NADH, and those seven rounds produce eight acetyl-CoA. Feed all eight through the citric acid cycle and run the reduced carriers through oxidative phosphorylation, and the books close at roughly 106 ATP. Compare that to glucose, which nets around 32 ATP per molecule. Per carbon, fat yields about 25% more ATP than sugar. That density is exactly why the body stores long-term energy as fat rather than carbohydrate.
